In summary, our research is concerned with
a number of questions.

the effects of a prolonged reading activity at two intensity levels on the following: vocal impact (measured by acoustic analysis of the voice), and self-rated vocal impact (self-ratings on a scale of 0-10, 0 = "no impact", 10 = "maximum impact").
the vocal impact of a prolonged, monotonous, and demanding reading task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no evidence that the vocal impact of a prolonged speech task is affected by the intensity level at which it is conducted, and that there is no indication that the subjective vocal effort rating is affected by intensity level.
the vocal impact of a prolonged (2 hours) reading task at a low intensity level (65 dBA) does not cause any significant changes in the voice.

a prolonged reading task, at two different intensity levels, does not cause a significant increase in vocal fatigue, as measured by the following parameters: maximum phonation time, jitter and shimmer, and the subjective ratings of voice and throat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of objective and subjective measurements of voice quality is a promising approach to investigate the effects of prolonged speech on the voice.
we found no difference between the two intensities in terms of objective vocal measures, while there were differences for the subjective measures of vocal fatigue and throat dryness.
we have shown that a reading task at a loud level is more stressful for the voice than the same reading task at a moderate level.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a lot of different factors that affect the quality of a reading task.
there are two main factors that influence the vocal impact of a prolonged speaking task.
there is no single optimal intensity for reading aloud.
